title: The Goal
author: Eliyahu M. Goldratt
theme: An organisation's performance is limited by a few constraints, so real improvement comes from identifying those bottlenecks and managing the whole system around them rather than optimising every part separately.
summary: The Goal is a business novel. Alex Rogo manages a struggling manufacturing plant where orders ship late, inventory piles up and costs keep rising. His division head gives him three months to turn things around or the plant will be closed. Under pressure at work and with his marriage under strain, Alex turns for help to Jonah, a physicist he once knew, who guides him with questions rather than answers.

Jonah first asks what the goal of the company actually is. Alex realises it is to make money, now and in the future, and that busy machines and high local efficiency do not guarantee it. Jonah offers three simpler measures: throughput, the rate at which the system earns money through sales; inventory, the money tied up in things meant to be sold; and operational expense, the money spent turning inventory into throughput.

On a hike with his son's scout troop, Alex sees how a line of walkers behaves like his plant. Each step depends on the one before, and ordinary variations in speed add up, so the whole group can move only as fast as its slowest member.

Back at work, Alex and his team find their bottlenecks, the resources with less capacity than demand. They learn that time lost at a bottleneck is lost for the entire plant, while time saved elsewhere changes little. So they keep bottlenecks working on the right jobs, check quality before parts reach them, shift load away from them and release new work in step with their pace.

Results improve quickly. Alex later steps back to turn these lessons into a repeatable way of thinking: find the constraint, make the most of it, align everything else to it, raise its capacity, and then look for the next one.
takeaway: Find the one constraint that limits your whole system, protect and strengthen it, and judge every decision by its effect on overall throughput.

questions.q: In what form is The Goal written?
options: A collection of academic case studies
A novel following a plant manager
A memoir of the author's career
A textbook of accounting rules
questions.why: Goldratt teaches his ideas through the story of Alex Rogo, who must save his failing manufacturing plant.

questions.q: According to the book, what is the goal of a manufacturing company?
options: To keep every machine and worker busy
To produce the highest number of parts
To cut costs as far as possible
To make money now and in the future
questions.why: Alex concludes that everything else, including efficiency and output, matters only if it helps the company make money.

questions.q: How does the book define throughput?
options: The rate at which the system generates money through sales
The number of parts a machine produces per hour
The total value of goods held in the warehouse
The cost of labour on the factory floor
questions.why: Throughput counts money earned through sales, not items produced that may simply sit in storage.

questions.q: What does Jonah mean by inventory?
options: Only finished goods awaiting shipment
The money spent on wages and utilities
The money the system has invested in things it intends to sell
The number of orders customers have placed
questions.why: Inventory is the money tied up in items meant for sale, which is why excess work-in-progress is a cost, not an achievement.

questions.q: What lesson does Alex learn from the scout hike?
options: Faster walkers should always lead the group
Taking frequent breaks raises overall speed
Each walker should set their own pace
Dependent steps and normal variation mean the group moves at the pace of its slowest member
questions.why: The hike shows how dependent events combined with statistical fluctuations limit the whole line to its slowest point.

questions.q: What is a bottleneck in the book's sense?
options: A resource whose capacity is equal to or less than the demand placed on it
Any machine that breaks down often
A department with too many workers
A supplier that charges high prices
questions.why: A bottleneck cannot keep up with the work required of it, so it sets the pace for the whole system.

questions.q: Why does an hour lost at a bottleneck matter so much?
options: It raises the cost of raw materials
It is an hour lost for the output of the entire system
It forces overtime in every department
It can always be recovered at other machines
questions.why: Because the bottleneck limits total output, any time it stands idle reduces throughput for the whole plant.

questions.q: What does the book suggest about saving time at a non-bottleneck resource?
options: It is the best way to raise profit
It should be rewarded with bonuses
It does little to improve overall output
It removes the need to manage bottlenecks
questions.why: Non-bottlenecks already have spare capacity, so making them faster does not increase what the system as a whole delivers.

questions.q: Which practice did Alex's team adopt to protect their bottlenecks?
options: Checking quality before parts reach the bottleneck
Running every machine at full speed all the time
Releasing as much new work as possible into the plant
Moving their best workers away from the bottleneck
questions.why: Inspecting parts before the bottleneck avoids wasting its scarce time on items that would later be scrapped.

questions.q: What is the final step in the improvement process Alex develops?
options: Close the plant's least efficient departments
Measure each worker's local efficiency
Increase inventory to protect against delays
Once a constraint is broken, go back and find the next one
questions.why: Improvement is ongoing: after one constraint is lifted, another becomes the limit and the cycle begins again.
